item.title: Russian missile hits Poland as Ukraine's allies hold military exercise, says Tusk
item.description:
To play this video you need to enable JavaScript in your browser.
This video can not be playedFigure caption,
Watch: CCTV shows explosion after Poland says airspace violated by Russian missileByPhoebe Hopson and Paul Kirby, Europe digital editorPublished20 November 2026, 12:09 GMTUpdated 2 hours ago
Poland says a Russian cruise missile was among three objects that violated its airspace early on Friday, with Prime Minister Donald Tusk saying it did not appear to be an accident when Western military exercises were taking place in the region.
Nobody was hurt and no damage has been reported, but Warsaw described the incident as a "provocation" from Moscow.
Russia has made no comment about the violations, which took place during one of its biggest aerial attacks on Ukraine since the start of the full-scale invasion in 2022.
Defence Minister Wladyslaw Kosiniak-Kamysz said the Kh-101 missile hit a rural area at Nowy Lipowiec in southeastern Poland about 50km (31 miles) from the Ukrainian border.
The cruise missile, designed for precision targets, crashed at about 06:30 (5:30GMT) and Natalie Szponar, a local resident, said she was getting her children ready for school when she heard a "whistle and a dull impact".
The moment of impact was caught by a camera on a farm, and officials later made clear there was no risk to residents.
Another suspected missile went down near Rudnik nad Sanem to the west of Nowy Lipowiec, and a jet-powered drone crashed to the south near Mołodycz, said Kosiniak-Kamysz.
He called the incursion into Polish airspace a "provocation" from Russia and said he would be asking Nato for additional support.
Nato Secretary General Mark Rutte condemned "grave violations of Polish airspace" and said Nato jets had been scrambled in response. "This incident is clearly dangerous - a consequence of Russia's ongoing war against Ukraine," said Rutte, who was due to visit Warsaw on Saturday.

item.title: Russia targets Kyiv crossings days after Ukraine hits Crimean Bridge
item.description:
Image source, ReutersImage caption,
Warehouses, railway stations, energy plants and residential buildings were hit during a night of heavy Russian strikesByDan Woodland and Sarah Rainsford, Eastern and Southern Europe correspondent, in KyivPublished20 November 2026, 08:04 GMTUpdated 3 hours ago
Russia targeted bridges in Kyiv and railway stations overnight in a major attack launched days after Ukraine badly damaged the strategically important Crimean Bridge.
Ballistic missiles hit key crossings in the capital during a nationwide assault which Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky said was "one of the most massive strikes" of the war so far and left at least nine dead.
Russian President Vladimir Putin had threatened to retaliate for the attack on the Crimean Bridge, which the Kremlin built to link Russia and the occupied Crimean peninsula.
The latest Russian strikes coincided with talks around the war, and came as the Kremlin pushed back against a US claim that Russia could be open to Western-backed security guarantees for Ukraine.
The overnight attack against Ukraine was spread across several cities and regions, Zelensky said, with residential buildings and energy facilities also hit.
Air raid sirens lasted non-stop throughout the night and were ongoing into the morning.
Zelensky said over 110 missiles and more than 400 attack drones were launched by Russia, adding that "particularly insidious" tactics to launch the waves in 20 to 30-minute internals made it "more difficult to extinguish fires, clear debris, and restore services".
The three bridges targeted in Kyiv - the Podilsko-Voskresensky Bridge, the Darnytskyi Bridge and the Southern Bridge - were closed to traffic.
Kyiv Mayor Vitali Klitschko urged people to "avoid travelling into the city by private car unless absolutely necessary", adding to the disruption around the capital following a first round of strikes against vital crossings earlier this week.

Watch: How did Anthropic's stock market debut unfold?ByRachel Clun and Jemma Crew, Business reportersPublished20 November 2026, 14:36 GMTUpdated 11 minutes ago
Anthropic's share price has dropped back towards its initial public offering (IPO) price a day after its soaring market debut, as the broader tech sell off continues.
The artificial intelligence (AI) company's introduction to the Nasdaq stock exchange on Thursday was a crucial test for the industry and was largely seen as a success, with trading starting at $111.50.
However, Anthropic's shares fell on Friday, dropping more than 10% to about $87.30, close to its IPO price of $83, and the broader stock market declines seen on Thursday continued.
The tech-heavy Nasdaq Composite Index fell 2.8% in morning trade, the S&P 500 was down 1.2% while the Dow Jones Industrial Average remained largely flat.
The maker of the Claude chatbot raised a record $81bn in its initial public offering (IPO), but its share price moved significantly in the first day of trading.
The shares peaked at $115 on Thursday, before easing to end the day up 17% at $97.17.
Analysts said volatility was to be expected in the first days or even weeks of Anthropic's trading, as the company was the first frontier AI firm to go public so had no direct peers.
Some have also noted the similarities with Elon Musk's SpaceX, which at the time of its debut in June was the largest IPO on record. Shares in the rocket and AI company experienced large swings in its first few weeks of trading.
Ed Moya, a strategist at market intelligence firm AlphaSense, said Anthropic's blockbuster IPO did not appear to have restored confidence in the broader AI market.

item.title: Nearly 600 women killed in South Africa within three months
item.description:
Image source, Gallo Images via Getty ImagesImage caption,
The killing of 13 women around Johannesburg earlier this year sparked a national outcryByKhanyisile NgcoboReporting fromJohannesburgPublished20 November 2026, 10:47 GMTUpdated 43 minutes ago
Nearly 600 women were killed in South Africa between July and September this year, according to the country's latest crime statistics.
This figure includes 13 women whose partially naked and bruised bodies were found dumped in public areas in and around Johannesburg.
The murders triggered national outrage and police faced pressure to find the culprits, in a country with one of the highest rates of gender-based violence and murder rates in the world.
In the latest shocking killing, five women and a toddler were gunned down in Free State province earlier this week.
The latest crime statistics, released on Friday, revealed that 581 women were killed in the country between July and September, including 131 in the Gauteng province which includes Johannesburg.
The same statistics revealed a slight decline in the number of murders.
Police reported 5,590 murders, 204 fewer than in the same period last year. This still come to an average of about 60 murders a day.
It is not clear whether the number of women killed is an increase or decrease because the police had stopped giving these figures recently due to what they said were "significant anomalies" in the statistics.
Grim discoveries of murdered women spark fear in South Africa
Published19 September
Acting Police Minister Firoz Cachalia said there needed to be "greater efforts to prevent... violence" against women and children.
According to police in Free State province, south of Johannesburg, three masked men opened fire on a family in the township of Botshabelo on Wednesday night.

item.title: Texas death-row inmate screams as execution takes more than one hour
item.description:
Image source, Houston Chronicle via Getty ImagesImage caption,
Reinaldo Dennes was convicted over the murder of a diamond dealer in 1996BySareen HabeshianPublished3 hours ago
A US death row inmate has screamed in apparent pain during his Texas execution which lasted more than an hour.
This is "not working the way it should be," Reinaldo Dennes, 70, said as he was being injected with the drug pentobarbital, according to witnesses.
A spokeswoman for the Texas Department of Criminal Justice said there had been unsuccessful attempts to find veins for the injections, but added that Dennes had reported pain in parts of his body where there were no attempted injections.
Dennes's case comes weeks after the botched execution of Christa Pike, who survived two lethal doses and is believed to be the only individual to have survived an execution attempt by lethal injection.
Dennes was sentenced to death over the 1996 murder of Janos Szucs, a diamond dealer who was found shot multiple times.
His execution came on the same day another inmate was put to death in Florida.
Executions with a lethal drug usually last from a few minutes to over an hour.
Michael Graczyk, an Associated Press reporter who has witnessed many such executions, described how they had waited for an unusually long time before being taken into the chamber. According to him, such delays are usually due to an inmate resisting the procedure or difficulty in finding veins.
When the witnesses were finally allowed in, Dennes almost immediately exclaimed, "The pain! Go! Go!", Graczyk said. He then uttered an expletive and asked "the father" to "take this pain".
He then shouted: "My right leg is killing me!", describing it as a cramp. After another expletive, he grunted and said, "I don't think this is normal."
Another witness, the reverend Jeff Hood, told USA Today that Dennes's execution was "by far the worst one" he had seen.

item.title: Catherine Zeta-Jones' daughter says parents warned her about 'nepo baby' label
item.description:
Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption,
Carys Douglas said her Oscar-winning parents taught her that "building my own identity depended on me and no one else"ByAngharad ThomasBBC WalesPublished44 minutes ago
Catherine Zeta-Jones's daughter has said her parents warned her people might have "preconceived notions" about her embarking on an acting career, as she shared her views on the "nepo baby" label.
Carys Douglas, 23, made her stage debut this year, playing the lead role of Nina in Anton Chekhov's The Seagull in Brooklyn, New York.
Zeta-Jones who is married to Michael Douglas, son of Hollywood star Kirk, previously said the "nepo baby" term was "horrific". It refers to children of famous parents perceived to have achieved riches and success off their parents' backs.
But the young actor said her parents taught her to build her "own identity" and that she has learned how to deal with the "pressure".
During an interview with Elle Spain, Carys Douglas said her parents "do not hide" from her that people would have preconceived ideas about her.
"They taught me that building my own identity depended on me and no one else. It was my responsibility, and it still is.
"As time has gone on, I've come to understand that there are different ways to deal with that kind of pressure," she said.
Her father, star of hit 1980s films such as Wall Street and Fatal Attraction, recently stated that he is not a fan of the "nepo baby" label, calling it an "unfortunate title".
"I guess you could say that about any business. The same thing with Hollywood royalty. My father's father was a junkman," Douglas, 82, said, referring to Kirk, who was considered a Hollywood Golden Age icon.
Zeta-Jones, 57, from Mumbles, Swansea, also criticised the phrase, saying it was "horrible because these kids didn't ask to be born into this, they're finding their own way in life".
"You have to go with your dreams, your passion," Zeta-Jones said.

How South Korea tackles cheating on its college entrance examByKoh EwePublished6 hours ago
South Korea's education ministry says 111 candidates were found with unauthorised smart devices during a high-stakes nationwide exam, after officials introduced urgent measures to tackle rising cases of AI-assisted cheating.
Five of the candidates were caught red-handed using smart devices during the exam, authorities said on Friday.
Half a million students sat for the college entry exam, also known as Suneung, which took place this week under the shadow of several recent high-profile cheating scandals.
Prior to the Suneung, authorities announced anti-cheating measures such as emergency alerts sent to every single mobile phone in the country to detect unauthorised devices in exam halls.
On Friday, Prime Minister Lee Jae Myung called for an overhaul of the exam system to tackle AI-assisted cheating.
In South Korea, public examinations "significantly affect the distribution of opportunities and resources", Lee said, adding that using AI to cheat in such tests "rocks the basic order of our society by undermining fairness and trust".
Concerns over academic dishonesty had been brewing in recent weeks, after reports of candidates cheating with the help of AI devices.
Last month, two candidates were caught cheating with AI glasses during university entrance exams.
The education ministry said earlier this month that four students across middle and high schools were caught using AI glasses to cheat this year.
These fears came to a boil over the weekend, when the top scorer of South Korea's certified tax accountancy exam admitted to cheating by using a miniature camera, mobile phone and AI tools.
His confession came amid speculation over his unusually high score, with just one out of 160 questions wrong.

item.title: White House removes cyber-security chief after series of tech outages
item.description:
Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption,
Sean Cairncross (left) was appointed by the Trump administrationByImran Rahman-JonesTechnology reporterPublished20 November 2026, 09:37 GMTUpdated 3 hours ago
The top cyber-security official in the US government is leaving his post after a little over a year in the job, US media report.
CBS, the BBC's US news partner, and other media report that White House National Cyber Director Sean Cairncross has been fired after losing the confidence of White House chief of staff Stephen Miller.
It comes after a string of tech outages which hit banking, air traffic control and other sectors.
US officials said the outages were not caused by cyberattacks but the blackouts had sparked scrutiny from members of Congress who demanded a clearer explanation of what went wrong.
There has been no official confirmation of the removal of Cairncross but Secretary of State Marco Rubio posted on X, external to say Department of Defense chief information officer Kirsten Davies was the new national cyber director.
The AFP news agency and CBS both said sources had told them Cairncross's sacking was supported by President Donald Trump. The BBC has asked the White House for comment.
The news, first reported by Axios, external, follows security concerns, including the ability of advanced AI models - mostly from US companies - to discover vulnerabilities which humans would not be able to find on their own.
Earlier this week, Rubio said there was "zero evidence" the outages were connected, adding "we are not under systemic attack".
But the fact that so many have happened in quick succession has left some people worried about the safety of the tech which is heavily relied on in all aspects of daily life.
Hacks, AI or just overdue updates - why have there been so many outages?

item.title: Massive hope for pancreatic cancer pill after trial saw tumours vanish
item.description:
Image source, Dr Michael May/Dr Wungki Park/Memorial Sloan Kettering Cancer Center/Press AssociationImage caption,
CT scans before (left) and after treatment with daraxonrasib plus chemotherapy (gemcitabine and nabpaclitaxel) showing multiple tumours that are no longer visible. Yellow arrows indicate the tumours visible before treatmentByMichelle RobertsDigital health editorPublished20 November 2026, 00:08 GMT
Experts are calling it the biggest breakthrough in pancreatic cancer treatment for decades - a daily pill that appears to shrink and possibly even eliminate tumours in some patients with one of the deadliest and hardest-to-treat cancers.
Cancer became undetectable on scans in one in 12 of the patients given daraxonrasib along with chemotherapy in early medical trials.
Tumours stopped growing in almost all of the 61 participants who had recently been diagnosed with advanced pancreatic cancer that had spread to other parts of the body.
But doctors stress it is unclear how long it might keep the disease at bay and should not be seen as a cure.
Incredibly exciting
Cancer Research UK called it "the biggest leap forward in decades" for pancreatic cancer patients.
The charity's Dr Sam Godfrey told BBC News that the results were incredibly exciting. "What this new drug has done is it's found a way of drugging the undruggable.
"We are finally seeing progress in pancreatic cancer which is so long overdue."
Pancreatic cancer is notoriously hard to treat and has the lowest survival rate of all common cancers in the UK.
Although chemotherapy can shrink tumours a bit, the cancer often grows again.
Most patients with advanced disease survive months, not years.
Doctors hope the new treatment might offer patients more time, even if it cannot stop cancers for good.
The trial followed patients for a year and a half, on average, and some did not see their cancer return during this time.

item.title: Nigeria moves to end jail terms for attempted suicide
item.description:
Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption,
The bill has been proposed by Nigeria's presidentByOndiro OgangaPublished20 November 2026, 06:32 GMT
Nigerian President Bola Tinubu has asked parliament to decriminalise attempted suicide, proposing medical support instead of prosecution for those who survive.
The proposal seeks to shift Nigeria's approach from criminal punishment to treatment and rehabilitation.
It follows years of calls for reform from mental health professionals. A separate bill seeking to decriminalise attempted suicide has already passed its second reading in the Senate.
Under Nigeria's law, attempted suicide is a criminal offence with those convicted facing up to one year's imprisonment, a fine or both.
The Senate bill also seeks to replace criminal penalties for attempted suicide with medical treatment, rehabilitation and support.
It was sponsored by Senator Asuquo Ekpenyong, who has argued that prosecuting people who survive suicide attempts could discourage those experiencing suicidal thoughts from seeking help.
He also warned that families might conceal such incidents for fear of prosecution and social stigma.
He stressed that the bill is not aimed at legalising or encouraging suicide attempts but rather protecting the survivors.
Tinubu's proposal has been welcomed by Senate President Godswill Akpabio, who had previously suggested that people who survived suicide attempts should be sent to prison.
"We are saying that suicide is a crime for now. Therefore, if you attempt it, we will send you to prison," Akpabio had said.
However, after receiving the Tinubu's proposal, he sought to clarify his earlier remarks, saying they did not apply to people experiencing mental health conditions.
He added that punishing people whose actions were influenced by mental health conditions would be insensitive.
Tinubu's letter follows sustained calls from mental health professionals for the law to be changed.
